text.p: MANCHESTER, July 4 (Reuter) The real Shane Warne stood up and England's batsmen were counted back to the Old Trafford pavilion on the second day of the third test on Friday.
Warne took five for 48 as England struggled to 161 for eight in reply to Australia's first innings 235.
Australian captain Mark Taylor has been telling anyone who will listen that Warne has not lost the ability to bamboozle even the best players, despite problems with his back and his spinning finger.
Another capacity crowd was forced to believe him as Warne ripped out England's middle-order to change the pattern of the match again.
From the comfort of 74 for one in mid-afternoon, the home team were reduced to 123 for eight soon after tea.
It required a stubborn, unbroken ninth-wicket stand between Mark Ealham (23 not out) and Andy Caddick (15 not out) to add a little more respectability to the score.
Warne's performance revived memories of his famous entry to test cricket in England four years ago on the same ground, spinning the ball prodigiously to bowl Mike Gatting with his first ball.

Ineffective in the first test of this series, he has steadily improved. His first ball of the England innings had Mark Butcher groping, and after Butcher (51) and his brother-in-law Alec Stewart (30) had their team thinking in terms of a substantial first innings lead, Warne broke through.
He had Stewart and Graham Thorpe taken at slip by Taylor, Nasser Hussain and John Crawley caught behind cheaply, and Darren Gough leg before.
Only the defiance of Ealham and Caddick prevented Warne finishing with even better figures.
Warne has now equalled fellow leg-spiner Richie Benaud's total of 248 wickets for Australia -- in eight fewer matches -- with only Craig McDermott (291) and Dennis Lillee (355) ahead of him.
"It's a great feeling and hopefully I can pass Richie in this game," said Warne. "I don't care whether people think I'm no good anymore, whether it's the public or the media."
It was also a good day for both wicketkeepers as the pitch slowly dried out in rare sunshine.

Australian Ian Healy's four dismissals, including a brilliant stumping of Butcher off Michael Bevan, took him past a century against England, and Stewart's two catches at the start of the day gave him six in the innings, equalling the Ashes record.
England coach David Lloyd was upset by the way his batsmen folded to Warne. "We went down like a pack of cards," he said. "They posed all the questions and we've got to be far more positive."
